abris.resume: Tarp, hammock, natural and emergency shelters: choose the shelter that suits the weather, put it up quickly and well, and sleep warm and dry in it.

p: A shelter isn't only for the rain. It cuts the wind (which can halve the felt temperature), keeps in body heat and insulates you from the ground. So a good shelter is small, waterproof, out of the wind and well insulated underneath.

encadre.texte: The smaller a shelter, the warmer it is. You build for your body, not for comfort.

sections.titre: Choosing a shelter for the weather
liste: Dry, mild weather: a simple roof or an open lean-to is enough, and lets you see the sky.
Rain: a low A-frame, well tensioned, with drip lines. Always insulate the ground well.
Wind: plough-point or very low A-frame, narrow end to the wind. Never an open lean-to facing the wind.
Cold: a small, low shelter that your own warmth can heat, with lots of ground insulation. A natural shelter covered with leaves is often warmer than a tarp.
Snow: a covered trench or the hollow at the foot of a spruce, with a vent that stays open.
Wet or sloping ground: the hammock, with insulation underneath and a tarp above.
A 3 × 3 m tarp: big enough for one person and their pack, light enough (400 to 900 g). With 3 × 4 m you can make a groundsheet.
At least 15 m of strong cord, in several pieces: 5 m for the ridgeline, the rest for the corners.
6 to 8 light pegs. You can also carve them on site from dead wood.
A groundsheet or a big bin bag, to protect the mat from damp.
A few bits of string for drip lines, and wide straps if you sleep in a hammock.

encadre.texte: Practise pitching your tarp in your garden or in a park, in daylight and then by head torch. On bivouac night, in the rain and the dark, the moves must be automatic.

p: A 3 × 3 m tarp and 15 m of cord allow many configurations. The most useful ones:
liste: The A-frame: cord stretched between two trees, tarp draped over it, edges pegged. Protects on all sides except the ends.
The lean-to: the tarp stretched as a slope on one side only, open towards the fire (where allowed). Good view, but exposed to wind.
The closed lean-to: like the lean-to, with one side folded down to the ground facing the prevailing wind.
The simple roof: tarp stretched flat with a slight slope, for shelter during the day or over a hammock.

encadre.texte: Tension the ridgeline with a trucker's hitch and adjust the guylines with taut-line hitches: the tarp won't flap in the wind.

p: Without gear, the forest provides everything. These shelters take time (1 to 3 hours) and energy: start them well before night. Keep them for real emergencies or for land where it is allowed, using dead wood only.
liste: The debris hut: a ridgepole resting on a stump, ribs on each side, and a thick layer of dead leaves. The warmest shelter without gear.
The branch lean-to: a pole between two trees, poles leaning against it, covered with branches like roof tiles.
Existing shelters: rock overhang, large fallen tree. Check they are stable and that no animal is living there.

The survival blanket: wrap yourself tightly in it, covering your head too. Which side (gold or silver) faces out matters little: what matters is being well wrapped, out of the wind and insulated from the ground.
The big bin bag: cut a hole for the head, and it becomes a poncho that blocks wind and rain.
The emptied backpack under your legs and feet, to insulate from the ground.
The hollow at the foot of a large conifer: the low branches form a natural roof.

encadre.texte: A survival blanket without ground insulation is not enough: you lose a lot of heat through contact with cold, wet ground.

sections.titre: A night without a sleeping bag
p: An unplanned night without a sleeping bag is handled with three priorities: insulate from the ground, protect from wind and trap air around the body. Dry dead leaves stuffed between two layers of clothing make a surprisingly effective insulator. The sheet “Spending the night without a sleeping bag” details what to do.

Whatever the shelter, the layer under your body matters as much as the roof. Dry dead leaves, ferns, pine needles or fine branches: you need 20 to 30 cm, because they compress under your weight. A layer that looks huge in the evening is often 5 cm by morning.

liste: Setting up too late: a shelter goes up in daylight. Aim for at least an hour before sunset.
Making it too big: a big shelter is cold and catches the wind. You build for your body.
Forgetting the ground: you can have a perfect roof and shiver all night from underneath.
Not looking up properly: a dead branch above the shelter is danger number one.
Pitching the tarp flat: water pools and ends up coming through. Always a slope.

encadre.texte: A good shelter is a good spot, a sloping roof, insulated ground and a small size. In that order.

feu.resume: Understand fire, light it even when wet, keep it going, cook and put it out. Always where it is allowed.

p: Fires in forests are forbidden or tightly controlled almost everywhere in Europe: in Wallonia, only at designated spots; in France, forbidden in woods and within 200 m of them for anyone who is not the owner, with total bans in summer in many départements. A stove remains the normal way to cook on a bivouac.
In a real emergency (hypothermia, unplanned night), a careful, controlled fire can save a life: it is then a survival tool, not a leisure activity.

encadre.texte: Never light a fire in a drought, in strong wind, under low branches, on peat, near the tent or inside a closed shelter.

p: A fire needs three things: fuel, heat and oxygen. If just one is missing, it goes out. Most failures come from fuel that is too big or too damp (not enough heat to catch) or a fire packed too tightly (not enough air).

liste: Tinder: what catches from a spark or a flame. Birch bark (burns even when damp thanks to its oils), dry grass, thistle or bulrush down, very fine shavings, cotton soaked in petroleum jelly (prepare it at home).
Kindling: twigs from the thickness of a match to that of a pencil. Dead twigs still on the tree, at the bottom of spruces, are the driest.
Fuel wood: from thumb to wrist thickness, then bigger. Only dead wood; wood that snaps cleanly with a dry crack is dry, wood that bends is damp.

encadre.texte: Prepare twice as much of each material as you need BEFORE lighting. Running off for wood while the flame dies means starting again.

liste: The lighter: the simplest. Keep it warm in an inside pocket (gas works badly in the cold).
Storm matches: burn even in the rain, keep them in a waterproof box.
The fire steel (ferrocerium): works wet and thousands of times. It needs very fine tinder.
A magnifying glass or the polished bottom of a can: only in bright sun.
Friction (bow drill): very difficult, needs perfectly dry wood and a lot of practice. Learn it at home, not on the day you need it.

p: The teepee is the ideal starting structure: the flame rises in the centre and catches the wood arranged in a cone. Once the fire has taken well, you can switch to a log cabin of crossed logs that gives lasting embers for cooking, or a star fire (big logs whose ends you push towards the centre) to last all night with little wood.
etapes: Clear the ground down to bare earth, or build a platform of sticks on wet ground.
Put the tinder in the centre, the finest kindling in a cone around it, open on the wind side.
Light it at ground level, shield the flame from the wind with your body.
Gradually add bigger wood without crushing the structure, blow gently at the base.

p: Depending on the weather and the use, other layouts do better than the teepee. Each has its own detailed sheet with a diagram:
liste: The lean-to fire: a green stick angled at 30° into the wind protects the tinder. Ideal in wind or drizzle.
The cross trench: a cross dug under the tinder creates a draught when there is no wind.
The pyramid: layers of crossed logs, lit from the top. The fire burns down slowly and heats all night without constant tending.
The Dakota hole: a buried fire with an air inlet. Discreet, not very sensitive to wind, economical with wood, perfect for a pot.
The reflector wall: logs stacked behind the fire send the heat back to you and cut the wind.

p: The “old-fashioned” methods work, provided you have practised them beforehand. They all rely on a good material that catches the ember.
liste: Char cloth: squares of cotton baked without air in a metal tin. It catches the smallest spark and is prepared at home for the survival kit.
Tinder fungus: this hoof-shaped fungus grows on dead beech and birch. Its felty layer, well dried and beaten, holds an ember for a long time.
The bow drill: a spindle spun with a bow on a board of soft wood until an ember forms. The most reliable friction method, but physical.
A magnifying glass or the polished bottom of a can: only in full sun.

encadre.texte: Keep a few squares of char cloth in a waterproof tin with your fire steel: it's the most reliable pair in all weathers.

liste: Look for dry material: dead twigs under conifers, birch bark, the inside of dead stumps.
Split dead wood: the heart is dry even when the outside is soaked.
Make feather sticks: carve long, thin curls without detaching them from the stick (see the Knife chapter).
Light the fire on a platform of sticks, not on wet earth.
Dry the next wood around the fire, without putting it in.
Warming up: a wall of logs, a rock face or a tarp behind the fire sends the heat back towards you (reflector fire).
Boiling water: the only truly safe improvised method.
Cooking: on the embers, not the flames (see the Cooking chapter).
Drying clothes and socks, at a reasonable distance: synthetics melt quickly.
Signalling: white smoke by day (add green leaves), a bright flame at night.

etapes: Stop adding wood an hour before leaving or sleeping.
Drown the embers with plenty of water.
Stir with a stick and drown again.
Hold the back of your hand above: no heat should be felt.
Scatter the cold ashes and erase the traces.

encadre.texte: An “extinguished” fire covered with earth can smoulder for hours underground and flare up again. Always drown and stir.

eau_guide.resume: How much to drink, recognising dehydration, finding water and making it safe to drink.

p: At rest and in mild weather, an adult needs about 2 to 3 litres of water a day. Effort, heat, dry cold and altitude greatly increase this need. It is better to drink small amounts often than a litre in one go.

encadre.texte: In survival, you don't ration the water you have: you ration sweating. Get into the shade, slow down, keep your head covered.

liste: Thirst, dry mouth, dark and scanty urine: drink without waiting.
Headache, tiredness, cramps, irritability: dehydration has set in.
Confusion, dizziness, no urine: emergency, call for help.
Springs, streams and rivers: prefer running water, upstream of villages, pastures and campsites.
Valley bottoms, greener and denser vegetation, insects and birds flying in the morning and evening often point to water.
Rainwater, collected with a tarp: the most generous improvised source.
Morning dew, collected with a cloth: a very limited extra.
Listed drinking water points: shown on Bivaska's map (“Drinking water” layer).

encadre.texte: Avoid stagnant water, water near cultivated fields (pesticides), roads or industrial sites, and seawater (which makes dehydration worse).

p: Even the clearest wild water can contain bacteria, viruses or parasites (such as Giardia) that cause severe diarrhoea, which then makes dehydration worse.
liste: Boiling: 1 minute at a rolling boil (3 minutes above 2,000 m). The only completely safe improvised method against germs.
Hiking filter: effective against bacteria and parasites, not always against viruses depending on the model.
Tablets (chlorine, chlorine dioxide): respect the stated waiting time, longer if the water is cold.
Pre-filtering (cloth, sand-charcoal filter): clears cloudy water but does not disinfect it. Always boil afterwards.
Without a pot: dry stones heated in the fire, dropped one by one into a container, will boil water (see the dedicated sheet).

encadre.texte: No improvised method removes chemical pollutants. If in doubt about where water comes from, look for another source.

p: When there is no running water, you can collect a little. According to a 2025 scientific review, here is what to expect:
liste: Rainwater: about 5 to 10 litres per shower with a tarp. By far the most worthwhile.
Transpiration bag on a branch: from a few decilitres to 1 litre a day, in the sun.
Solar still (hole + plastic): 0.3 to 0.6 litres a day, spending a lot of energy digging. Rarely worthwhile in our climates.
Dew: about a glass. Just a supplement.

nourriture.resume: Why food comes after everything else, foraging without poisoning yourself, and what the law says.

sections.titre: A low priority… but not zero
p: A healthy adult can last several weeks without eating. On a bivouac of a few days, hunger is mainly a matter of comfort and morale. On the other hand, eating helps fight the cold: in cold weather, the body needs much more energy to keep its temperature up.
So the real survival rule is to bring your own food: energy-dense foods (dried fruit, nuts, chocolate, hard cheese, pasta, oat flakes), and an emergency reserve that is never touched.

etapes: Only eat what you identify with absolute certainty, checking several features (leaves, stem, flower, smell, habitat), never just one.
Know the dangerous look-alikes of each species: that is what each Bivaska sheet is for.
Never rely on a single photo or an identification app.
Avoid the whole umbellifer family (umbrella-shaped flowers): several are deadly and they all look alike.
Start with a small amount of a species new to you, even an edible one (allergies, intolerances).
Wash or cook what grows at ground level (parasites spread by foxes), and avoid roadsides and treated fields.

p: Some military manuals describe a test that involves rubbing a plant on the skin, then the lip, then chewing a little and waiting several hours. In Europe, this test is dangerous: hemlock, hemlock water-dropwort or yew can kill in small doses, even before the test's symptoms appear. And it doesn't apply to mushrooms at all.

encadre.texte: Never taste an unknown plant or mushroom “to see”. No certainty, no picking.

liste: Easy fruits with no dangerous look-alike: blackberries, raspberries, bilberries, wild strawberries, hazelnuts, sweet chestnuts (checking against horse chestnut).
Abundant, safe leaves: nettle (cooked), dandelion, plantain, wild garlic (with extreme caution regarding lily of the valley and autumn crocus).
Autumn and winter fruits: rose hips, sloes after the frosts, roasted beechnuts.
Wetlands: bulrush (shoots and cooked rhizomes), only in clean water, being wary of yellow flag iris.
Mushrooms: only if a mycologist has checked the harvest. In a real survival situation, the energy they provide isn't worth the risk.

p: Rich in protein, they are the most accessible and safest animal resource in a real emergency. Grasshoppers, locusts, crickets and wood grubs are always eaten cooked (roasted), with legs and wings removed. Avoid brightly coloured, hairy or stinging insects or those that smell strongly, as well as caterpillars.

sections.titre: Fishing, hunting and traps: the law
p: In Belgium as in France, Switzerland or Germany, fishing requires a licence or a fishing permit, and hunting or setting traps without authorisation is poaching. The snares and deadfalls described in survival manuals should therefore only be considered in a real life-threatening emergency, and dismantled before you leave.
